findings.title: ReDoS in HTML element detection via attacker-set Symbol.toStringTag
findings.description: Entry: source/index.ts:195 (the exported `detect`/`is(value)`; the same regex also runs from every specific guard, e.g. is.date at source/index.ts:554 and is.regExp at source/index.ts:866, and from typeErrorMessage at source/index.ts:1000). Attacker: the supplier of an untrusted value that the application passes to `is()`, for example user-controlled code in a sandbox or plugin that hands host code an object whose `Symbol.toStringTag` it sets, crossing the boundary that this validation library is expected to inspect hostile values without doing unbounded work. Path: detect (source/index.ts:195) calls getObjectType(value) (source/index.ts:245), which builds objectTypeName from Object.prototype.toString.call(value).slice(8, -1) (source/index.ts:182) - that string is exactly value[Symbol.toStringTag], fully attacker-chosen - and then runs /HTML\w+Element/v.test(objectTypeName) (source/index.ts:184). Nothing on the path stops it: the tag is read with no length cap, the pattern is unanchored, and \w+ is greedy, so a tag such as 'HTML'.repeat(n) makes the engine start an attempt at each of the ~n/4 'HTML' occurrences, and at each attempt \w+ consumes the remaining O(n) characters and then backtracks O(n) times looking for the literal Element, i.e. O(n^2) regex steps for a single value; the checks that run before it (isObservable and isBuffer) do not reject a plain object carrying a custom Symbol.toStringTag, so control reaches the regex with the attacker's string intact. Impact: O(n^2) CPU time per call on attacker-controlled input; a long tag (e.g. 10^6 characters) pins a CPU core for seconds and repeated calls produce a denial-of-service in any service that validates untrusted values. Fix: anchor and bound the pattern, e.g. test /^HTML\w+Element$/v (or /^HTML\w{0,256}Element$/v), or drop the regex entirely and compare the tag directly (objectTypeName.startsWith('HTML') && objectTypeName.endsWith('Element') with a length guard), or cap objectTypeName.length before running the test.
